title: He is with you wherever you are
hook: He is with you wherever you are (57:4)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the end of Al-Waqi'ah: mutahharun, the purified, and your line, touched with purity. Today, Surah Al-Hadid, the Iron.

An airport gate at 5am. A hospital corridor. A new apartment with the boxes still taped shut. A hotel room in a city where you don't speak the language. Places like these can make a person feel strangely unhooked, as if they've left their whole life at the last address. Surah fifty-seven, Al-Hadid, has a short line for exactly that feeling. It sits in the middle of a verse about the heavens and the Throne.

Al-Hadid opens wide: everything in the heavens and the earth glorifies God. Verse three gives four names in a row: he is the First and the Last, the Outward and the Inward. Verse four describes God creating the heavens and the earth in six days, then establishing himself on the Throne. He knows what goes into the earth and what comes out, what comes down from the sky and what goes up into it. And then, in Pickthall: "and He is with you wheresoever ye may be." Wa huwa ma'akum ayna ma kuntum. Ma'akum: with you. Ayna ma kuntum: wherever you are. The verse ends: and God sees what you do. So how is God with you? Muslims have explained it in more than one way. Commentators such as Ibn Kathir said he is with you by his knowledge, hearing and sight, watching over you, while being above his Throne, as the same verse says. Others, among them Sufi writers, dwell on the nearness itself, and read it with another verse: God is nearer to a person than their jugular vein. Both readings agree on one thing: in the verse, no place is out of his sight. The hadith of Jibril turns this into a way of worshipping. Asked what ihsan, excellence, is, the Prophet ﷺ said: to worship God as though you see him, and if you don't see him, he sees you. The airport gate, the hospital, the empty apartment: the verse doesn't make them less strange. It says you didn't arrive there alone.
screen: `THE FIRST, THE LAST, OUTWARD, INWARD.` · `WITH YOU, WHEREVER YOU ARE.` · `BY KNOWLEDGE AND SIGHT, OR NEARNESS.` · `IHSAN: AS THOUGH YOU SEE HIM.`

segments.voice: Feel exactly where you are: the floor, the chair, the air on your skin. Breathe in: wherever; breathe out: you are. Then picture the next unfamiliar place you'll walk into, a waiting room, a new street, and hear the line said quietly at its door.
Ma'akum: with you, the words of 57:4 that say God is with a person wherever they are. Today's word.
Your line: wherever you are. Even at an airport gate at 5am. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some Muslims recall this verse when traveling or in unfamiliar places; the idea of ihsan, worshipping as though one sees God, is taught from the hadith of Jibril, where it follows islam and iman.

trapdoor: what you thought: a comforting line about God being everywhere.
what it means: in a verse about the Throne, God says he is with you wherever you are, and sees what you do.
what a scholar hears: ma'iyya, divine 'withness', read by Ibn Kathir and others as knowledge and oversight, by Sufi readers as nearness, alongside 50:16; ihsan from the hadith of Jibril (Muslim 8).

chat.says: I just moved somewhere new and feel totally alone. Does Islam say anything about that?
options: Al-Hadid says He is with you wherever you are, even somewhere new.
God is close only in a mosque; elsewhere you'll have to wait.
God is with you only in the city where you grew up.
chat.meaning: 57:4: and He is with you wheresoever ye may be. Commentators say by knowledge and sight, or dwell on nearness; no place is out of His sight.
